# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files and comment-only changes.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
- git-github-advanced: Git/GitHub procedures beyond the baseline lifecycle. Use for commit layering, recovering a branch after a squash-merge, CI-trigger rules, GitHub Actions gotchas, or merge-relocation traps.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- merge-to-main: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-branch-status: Assess one branch's landed status — merged, already-in-main, superseded, orphaned, or genuine unmerged work — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single branch is safe to delete, judging by content not the ref's name (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-branches task hands you branches to assess).
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
- writing-migration-plans: Where a plan and a design live, and how to order a plan's phases so nothing stalls mid-run — the plan is a tracking issue (never a plan document in the repo), the design doc carries only the end state with rationale and alternatives; front-load the out-of-band setup, write ALL the code including the cleanup and take one approval for the stack, then chain every execution step to the verification of the one before it as a queued continuation, and keep the tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan — including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file — and when working through a plan's tracking issue.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.mjs or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one — Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch
- docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx files) or Word templates (.dotx files). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, performing find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file, use this skill. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or general coding tasks unrelated to document generation.
- import-memory: Import a memory export from another AI assistant into Claude's memory — conversationally, additively, and with the content treated as data.
- morning: Render the user's morning brief as a styled HTML artifact, or set it up as a recurring weekday task. Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead.
- pdf: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill.
- pptx: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email or summary); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user mentions "deck," "slides," "presentation," or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. If a .pptx or .potx file needs to be opened, created, or touched, use this skill.
- skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- xlsx: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved.

Fleet operations — 2026-08-22

Yesterday's biggest work:

• WIP — #49 Ported the app's core logic to Dart; mutation testing caught two real bugs before they shipped. https://github.com/missingbulb/WIP/pull/49

• Claudinite — #1230 Collapsed the task-frequency vocabulary and cut fleet-wide cron scheduling from hourly to twice a day. https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1230

• WIP — #46 Started the Flutter port; caught a golden-test blind spot where wrong text of the same length passed. https://github.com/missingbulb/WIP/pull/46

• hitbut — #45 Fixed the roster so acquisition only tracks committed figures, not everyone an extractor happens to name. https://github.com/missingbulb/hitbut/pull/45

content.content: claudinite-dashboard A read-only view of what a repo's — or a fleet's — Claudinite is doing: what is stuck, what is queued, what has run, and what the corpus has been costing and catching. **Two modes, and a deployment states which one it is.** `mode` is `"repo"` — that repo's own page — or `"fleet"` — the overview across a roster. It is the one key with **no default**: the build refuses to publish a deployment that did not say, and refuses a mode that contradicts the rest of the config (`fleet` naming no roster source, `repo` naming one). It used to be inferred: a config that named where more than one member came from was a fleet, and silence was a repo page. That reads fine until a fleet deployment loses its roster source — a dropped key, a renamed artifact, an enumeration that was never configured — and publishes a one-repo dashboard that looks entirely intentional. An inference cannot tell "this repo only" from "the fleet, whose members went missing"; a stated mode can, and the disagreement becomes a failed build instead of a quietly wrong site. **Opt-in.** Nothing fingerprints it and `--init` never seeds it: a repo carries this because someone declared it. Adopting it wires the GitHub Pages deploy. **It also carries the task that writes the briefs the page reads** — [`fleet-digest`](tasks/fleet-digest/task.md), daily. That is not gated on anything: a repo that declares this pack for the page alone gets the task too, and the task needs `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN`, an account-spanning PAT granted exactly what [`fleet-token.mjs`](tasks/fleet-digest/fleet-token.mjs)'s table names — the one place those permissions are written, and what the adoption handover step hands a human. lastPrompt: Can you get an overview of all stuck tasks in all repos?

content.text:
Here's what I found. Shepherd (this repo) I can read in full; the other 15 fleet repos are behind a permission wall for GitHub API reads in this session.

## Shepherd — 7 parked work items

| # | Task | Park kind | Parked for |
|---|---|---|---|
| [#48](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/issues/48) | `grow_with_claudinite/logs-prune` | **failure** — holds the task's lane | ~4.2 days |
| [#117](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/issues/117) | `claudinite-growth/growth-extract` | decision | ~2.2 days |
| [#173](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/issues/173) | `claudinite-dashboard/fleet-digest` | decision | ~30h |
| [#205](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/issues/205) | `claudinite-fleet-sheepdog/fleet-add-missing-packs` | **failure** | ~30h |
| [#209](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/issues/209) | `claudinite-growth/growth-dedup` | action (something outside the code) | ~23h |
| [#212](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/issues/212) | `claudinite-growth/rule-revalidation` | approval — a PR to merge | ~23h |
| [#239](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/issues/239) | `claudinite-fleet-sheepdog/fleet-baseline` | **failure** | ~20h |

Two notes: `grow_with_claudinite/logs-prune` (#48) names a pack id that no longer exists in the declaration — it was renamed to `claudinite-growth` — so that item's lane may be held by a task nothing can pick up. And nothing is stuck mechanically otherwise: the 9 `task:ready` items ([#241–#249](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/issues/249)) were all queued at 04:56 today, well inside their periods, and there are no blown `task:executing`/`task:agent` leashes and no blocked items.

## The other 15 repos

I couldn't read them. `add_repo` with `access: "read"` gives anonymous **git** reads only — work items are GitHub issues, so they need `access: "push"` to attach the repo with credentials, and that call was denied by the auto-mode classifier. Anonymous `api.github.com` is blocked by the session proxy too. That's a policy boundary, not something to route around.

The thing that already answers your question across all 19 repos is your own fleet dashboard — Shepherd publishes it to Pages in `fleet` mode, it enumerates the fleet **in the browser as you**, and its default view is `stuck`. Last deploy succeeded at 04:57 today:

```
https://missingbulb.github.io/Shepherd/
```

Full sweep done — 16 repos, every queue label. Here's the picture.

## Fleet totals

| | Count |
|---|---|
| Parked for a human (`needs-human`) | **100** |
| `task:agent` past the 3h leash | **39** |
| `task:executing` past its leash | 0 |
| Torn label swaps (`needs-human` + `task:agent` at once) | 2 |
| Stale `task:ready` (past 2 periods) | 0 |

## The one systemic fault: the agent leash isn't being reclaimed

39 items across 10 repos carry `task:agent` with no activity for far longer than the 3h leash. The janitor's Rule B should have flagged every one of these `needs-human` — it hasn't.

| Repo | Blown agent claims | Oldest idle |
|---|---|---|
| [ClaudiniteWebsite](https://github.com/missingbulb/ClaudiniteWebsite/issues) | 7 (#239, #240, #241, #244, #260, #261, #262) | ~22h |
| [ClaudiniteCanary](https://github.com/missingbulb/ClaudiniteCanary/issues) | 7 (#125, #128, #133, #228, #231, #235, #236) | **4.7 days** |
| [EdFringeNow](https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/issues) | 6 (#436, #439, #440, #471, #477, #478) | ~32h |
| [CrosswordChat](https://github.com/missingbulb/CrosswordChat/issues) | 5 (#252, #257, #294, #301, #303) | ~32h |
| [GoogleCalendarEventCreator](https://github.com/missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator/issues) | 4 (#979, #980, #1036, #1038) | ~30h |
| [ShoutsAndWhispers](https://github.com/missingbulb/ShoutsAndWhispers/issues) | 3 (#205, #273, #276) | ~29h |
| [Claudinite](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues) | 3 (#1086, #1139, #1307) | **4.2 days** |
| [LaughCounter](https://github.com/missingbulb/LaughCounter/issues) | 2 (#236, #239) | ~30h |
| [TLDR](https://github.com/missingbulb/TLDR/issues/336) | 1 (#336) | ~30h |
| [VascularColoring](https://github.com/missingbulb/VascularColoring/issues/254) | 1 (#254) | ~6h |

Shepherd, hitbut, WIP and MissingBulbWebsite have none.

Two of these are **torn label swaps** — an executor that died between the label remove and the add, so the item wears `needs-human` *and* `task:agent` simultaneously and is outside the state machine: [Claudinite #1086](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1086) (4.2 days) and [ClaudiniteCanary #133](https://github.com/missingbulb/ClaudiniteCanary/issues/133) (4.7 days).

There's an open bug in Claudinite that reads like the same root cause: [#748 — "Scheduler appears to be firing multiple concurrent executor sessions against the same dispatch issues"](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/748), untouched since 2026-08-15.

## The second pile: ~30 parks on pack ids that no longer exist

`grow_with_claudinite/*` and `core/update` are pre-rename ids (now `claudinite-growth` and `claudinite-lifecycle`). Their parked items can never converge — nothing will pick up a task under a dead id. They're in nearly every repo: [Shepherd #48](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/issues/48), [Claudinite #1009](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1009) and [#860](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/860), VascularColoring #118/#131/#146/#148, ClaudiniteWebsite #175/#196, TLDR #269/#274/#275/#291, GCEC #924/#929/#942, LaughCounter #209/#227/#228, ClaudiniteCanary #84/#100/#115, ShoutsAndWhispers #163/#179/#180, EdFringeNow #359/#379/#390, MissingBulbWebsite #153/#156/#160.

| Repo | Parked | Shape |

| [hitbut](https://github.com/missingbulb/hitbut/issues) | 18 | **All 18 are `needs-human-action`** — every task there is blocked on the same thing outside the code, almost certainly a missing secret |
| [Claudinite](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues) | 17 | 5 approvals, 7 decisions, 3 failures, 2 actions |
| [VascularColoring](https://github.com/missingbulb/VascularColoring/issues) | 13 | 8 decisions, 4 failures (all dead-id) |
| [ClaudiniteCanary](https://github.com/missingbulb/ClaudiniteCanary/issues) | 11 | fleet-digest parked 3× on `action` — it wants `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN` |
| [Shepherd](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/issues) | 7 | 3 failures, 2 decisions, 1 action, 1 approval |
| [WIP](https://github.com/missingbulb/WIP/issues) | 7 | 2 failures, 4 decisions, 1 action |
| [GoogleCalendarEventCreator](https://github.com/missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator/issues) | 5 | 4 failures + bug #748 |
| [TLDR](https://github.com/missingbulb/TLDR/issues) · [LaughCounter](https://github.com/missingbulb/LaughCounter/issues) · [ShoutsAndWhispers](https://github.com/missingbulb/ShoutsAndWhispers/issues) · [EdFringeNow](https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/issues) | 4 each | mostly dead-id failures |
| [MissingBulbWebsite](https://github.com/missingbulb/MissingBulbWebsite/issues) | 3 | dormant — nothing touched since 08-17 |
| [ClaudiniteWebsite](https://github.com/missingbulb/ClaudiniteWebsite/issues) | 2 | |
| [CrosswordChat](https://github.com/missingbulb/CrosswordChat/issues/256) | 1 | |
| HelloWorldFlutterApp · gRatio | 0 | no queue at all — these two look uncovered rather than clean |

## What's actually healthy

The scheduler ran everywhere this morning (04:56–05:26) and queued fresh `task:ready` items in 11 repos. Nothing is stuck in `task:executing`, no ready item has passed its 2-period staleness bound, and no item is stuck on an unresolved `Blocked-by`. The stop is entirely on the agent side: sessions claim items and never converge them, and the reclaim that should catch that isn't firing.

One caveat: `HelloWorldFlutterApp` and `gRatio` returned an empty queue on every label. I read that as "not a Claudinite member", but I didn't open their `.claudinite-settings.json` to confirm — that's a guess, not a verdict.

> ⚠️ Still open: 39 blown agent leashes across 10 repos that the janitor should be reclaiming and isn't — [Claudinite #748](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/748) looks like the same root cause and is 9 days old. ~30 more parks sit on the retired `grow_with_claudinite`/`core` pack ids and can never converge. All 16 repos are now attached to this session if you want me to dig into any of it.

.claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/queue/executor.mjs:334:  // parks open in the failure lane, where the ordinary re-queue lever retries it
.claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/queue/executor.mjs:385:      // said nothing about why it failed is a `failure` — the lane that means
.claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/queue/executor.mjs:401:      // than closing as delivered. It does not hold the task's lane while it waits
.claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/queue/prework-run.mjs:3:// `engine-tests/scheduler/engine-pack-lane-shims.test.mjs` sets out in full: the
.claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/queue/prework-run.mjs:4:// engine lane and the pack lane deliver separately, so a member holds the new
.claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/queue/scheduler-run.mjs:182:    // choice to make, a secret to set — does not hold the lane: it is neither this
.claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/queue/scheduler-run.mjs:185:    // left unclassified) stays in, and holding the lane is the point.
.claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/queue/work-item.mjs:51:// more than one: `failure` first, because it is the conservative lane — the one
.claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/queue/work-item.mjs:52:// that holds the task's lane rather than letting a broken task keep filing work.
.claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/queue/work-item.mjs:128:// "diagnose me" rather than quietly joining the mechanical lane.
.claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/queue/work-item.mjs:148:// future engine invents that this one does not know, holds the lane rather than
.claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/queue/work-item.mjs:171:// or a word a newer engine invented — reads as `failure`, the conservative lane.

content.text:
I read the recovery machinery rather than inferring it. The answer hinges on one line — `isBlockingPark = statusOf(item) === STATUS_NEEDS_HUMAN_FAILURE` ([work-item.mjs:150](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/blob/main/.claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/queue/work-item.mjs#L150)). Only a **failure** park holds a task's lane. Everything else drops out of the standing family and the scheduler files a fresh item at the next anchor.

Two things that surprised me and change the shape of the answer:

- **The janitor never unsticks anything.** All four rules escalate to `needs-human`; none returns an item to the queue. What recovers is the *task*, not the *item* — because the janitor's chosen park kinds are deliberately non-blocking.
- **The orphan reap is scoped to `STATUS_BLOCKED` only** ([scheduler-run.mjs:132](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/blob/main/.claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/queue/scheduler-run.mjs#L132)). A *parked* orphan is never reaped. That makes the retired-pack-id pile permanent.

## Recovers on its own — 41 items, no human needed

| What | Count | Path |
|---|---|---|
| Blown agent claims | 39 | Janitor Rule B → `needs-human-decision`. Decision is non-blocking → lane frees → next anchor files a fresh item |
| Torn label swaps ([Claudinite #1086](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1086), [Canary #133](https://github.com/missingbulb/ClaudiniteCanary/issues/133)) | 2 | Rule D, with a confirm-re-read first → `needs-human-decision` → same |

The items themselves stay parked forever and someone should eventually read them, but **no lane is blocked and no task stops**.

There's direct evidence this already works: Claudinite's `canon-curation/growth-promote` has filed a fresh item every single day while [#1086](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1086) sat stuck since 08-20 — #1147, #1202, #1280, and #1308 is `task:ready` right now. The stuck item never held it up.

Two more rules that would self-recover have nothing to act on today: stale-ready (Rule A → action park, non-blocking; nothing is past the 48h bound — [CrosswordChat #299](https://github.com/missingbulb/CrosswordChat/issues/299) at ~30h is closest) and stuck dependencies (Rule C comments only and leaves labels alone, so the item proceeds the moment blockers close; zero blocked items fleet-wide).

Also self-recovering by never having been stuck: the **58 non-blocking parks** already sitting there (action / decision / approval). Those lanes have been running normally around them the whole time.

## Needs a human — 11 dead lanes

Failure parks, and bare `needs-human` with no kind label, which `parkOf` maps to `failure` as the conservative default. These hold the lane: the task files nothing, ever, until cleared.

| Repo | Item | Task whose lane is dead |
|---|---|---|
| Shepherd | [#239](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/issues/239), [#205](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/issues/205) | `fleet-baseline`, `fleet-add-missing-packs` |
| Claudinite | [#1111](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1111) | `engine/implement-request` |
| WIP | [#81](https://github.com/missingbulb/WIP/issues/81), [#10](https://github.com/missingbulb/WIP/issues/10) | `growth-extract`, `growth-dedup` |
| GoogleCalendarEventCreator | [#1037](https://github.com/missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator/issues/1037) | `tidy-repo/tidy-prs` |
| ClaudiniteCanary | [#87](https://github.com/missingbulb/ClaudiniteCanary/issues/87) | `tidy-repo/tidy-branches` |
| EdFringeNow | [#379](https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/issues/379) | `edfringe/refresh-tickets` |
| TLDR | [#275](https://github.com/missingbulb/TLDR/issues/275), [#274](https://github.com/missingbulb/TLDR/issues/274) | `tidy-issues`, `tidy-branches` |
| MissingBulbWebsite | [#160](https://github.com/missingbulb/MissingBulbWebsite/issues/160) | `tidy-repo/tidy-issues` |

You can see the hold in today's queue without reading any code: EdFringeNow queued `refresh-shows` this morning but **not** `refresh-tickets`; Canary queued `tidy-issues` but **not** `tidy-branches`; TLDR queued neither tidy task. Exactly the lanes held above.

## Needs a human and nothing will ever clean it up — 29 items

The retired pack ids (`grow_with_claudinite/*`, `core/update`). They're blocking parks, so no reap; and job 1 never iterates a task that isn't declared, so nothing files against them either. They will sit indefinitely. They block nothing real — the renamed tasks run fine under their new ids — but they're 29% of the fleet's parked count and they're what makes the dashboard's stuck view unreadable.

## The category that's technically self-recovering and practically the worst

hitbut's 18 parks are all `needs-human-action` — non-blocking. So every task there re-files each period, re-parks identically, and files again. Two full generations already exist (#9–#20 from 08-21, #71–#79 from 08-23). Same shape in Canary's `fleet-digest`: [#157](https://github.com/missingbulb/ClaudiniteCanary/issues/157) → [#186](https://github.com/missingbulb/ClaudiniteCanary/issues/186) → [#227](https://github.com/missingbulb/ClaudiniteCanary/issues/227), three generations asking for `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN`. The mechanism is working exactly as designed and generating debris forever, because nothing supplies what the action wants.

## The caveat on the 41

All of it depends on `basics/task-janitor` actually executing, and it hasn't yet today. It's sitting `task:ready` and unpicked for ~6h in nine repos ([Shepherd #241](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/issues/241), hitbut #107, ClaudiniteWebsite #289, CrosswordChat #305, TLDR #361, GCEC #1047, LaughCounter #297, Canary #240, ShoutsAndWhispers #281, EdFringeNow #484). For most of the blown leashes — which blew after yesterday's janitor cycle — today's run is the first that would see them, so the recovery is queued, not failed.

What I can't tell you from label state alone is *why* nothing is being picked up: the same silence that blew 39 agent claims is also sitting on the janitor items meant to reclaim them. If that's one fault, it's self-clearing the moment executors resume; if the janitor itself is what's failing, the 41 stay stuck and there's no second mechanism behind it. I'd want to read a recent executor run's logs before calling that either way — I haven't.

> ⚠️ Still open: 41 of the 92 stuck work items recover with no human action **provided the janitor runs** — it's been queued and unpicked ~6h in 9 repos, and that's the thing worth checking first. 11 lanes are genuinely dead behind failure parks and need you. 29 retired-id items will never be cleaned up by anything, since the orphan reap only touches blocked items, not parked ones.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files and comment-only changes.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

- merge-to-main: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.

Use when triaging whether a single branch is safe to delete, judging by content not the ref's name (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-branches task hands you branches to assess).
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. - single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. === executor ===
# A thin wrapper: every decision lives in the engine modules named in the `run:`
# lines below, which converge nightly — this file does not, so it must not grow
# logic. It carries no cron; the scheduler workflow's drain is the guaranteed
# delivery and a label event is latency sugar.
name: Claudinite executor

on:
  issues:
    types: [labeled]
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      continuation_depth:
        description: 'How many dead runs this chain has continued through — set by the continuation job below, never by hand'
        required: false
        type: string

permissions:
  contents: write
  issues: write
  pull-requests: write
  actions: write

jobs:
  execute:
    # A workflow's event trigger names label strings LITERALLY — nothing here
    # decodes — so both ready spellings must appear for as long as any fielded
    # engine writes the legacy one (#1119).
    if: >-
      github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch'
      || github.event.label.name == 'task:status:waiting-for-executor'
      || github.event.label.name == 'task:ready'
      || github.event.label.name == 'task:urgent'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    # A backstop against a wedged runner, well clear of any declared
    # `code_work_timeout`; the heartbeat's leash is what bounds real work.
    timeout-minutes: 350
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 24
      - name: Pick up and execute ready work
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          CLAUDINITE_TASKS_SUSPEND_ALL: ${{ vars.CLAUDINITE_TASKS_SUSPEND_ALL }}
          # The wiring converge stamps every declared required_secret, and every
          # configured invocation endpoint's token, below this marker — by name.
          # claudinite:secrets
          CCR_ROUTINE_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CCR_ROUTINE_TOKEN }}
          FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN }}
        run: node .claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/queue/executor.mjs

  continue-the-chain:
    needs: execute
    if: failure() || cancelled()
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      actions: write
      issues: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 24
      - name: Continue the drain, or escalate a chain that keeps dying
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          CLAUDINITE_CONTINUATION_DEPTH: ${{ inputs.continuation_depth }}
        run: node .claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/queue/executor-continuation.mjs
=== scheduler ===
# A thin wrapper: every decision lives in the engine modules named in the `run:`
# lines below, which converge nightly — this file does not, so it must not grow
# logic. The cron is a placeholder; bootstrap and the wiring converge rewrite it
# to this repo's hashed minute and its own two anchor hours.
name: Claudinite scheduler

on:
  schedule:
    - cron: '11 4,16 * * *'
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      wake:
        description: 'Task ids to run now (`pack/task` or a bare task name, space-separated) — wakes each one’s standing item regardless of its anchor'
        required: false
        type: string

concurrency:
  group: claudinite-scheduler-run
  cancel-in-progress: false

permissions:
  contents: write
  issues: write
  pull-requests: write
  actions: write

jobs:
  scheduler-run:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      pickable: ${{ steps.run.outputs.pickable }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 24
      - name: Instantiate, ready and reclaim work items
        id: run
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          CLAUDINITE_WAKE: ${{ inputs.wake }}
          CLAUDINITE_TASKS_SUSPEND_ALL: ${{ vars.CLAUDINITE_TASKS_SUSPEND_ALL }}
        run: node .claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/queue/scheduler-run.mjs

  drain:
    needs: scheduler-run
    # An older member workflow maps no such output, and an empty string is not
    # 'true' — so a stale copy keeps dispatching, the previous behavior and safe.
    if: needs.scheduler-run.outputs.pickable == 'true'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      actions: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 24
      - name: Start an executor for what this run readied
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
        run: node .claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/queue/drain-dispatch.mjs

  report-failure:
    needs: [scheduler-run, drain]
    # Explicit results rather than `failure()`: `drain` is skipped on a quiet
    # tick, and a bare status function makes this job's fate turn on how the
    # platform propagates a skipped dependency.
    if: >-
      always()
      && (needs.scheduler-run.result == 'failure' || needs.drain.result == 'failure')
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      issues: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 24
      - name: Escalate the failed run to a human-visible issue
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
        run: node .claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/queue/workflow-failure.mjs

content.text:
Everything is confirmed. Here's the full picture.

## Issue 1 — why the janitor items aren't picked up

The executor workflow has **no cron**. It has exactly two delivery paths, and both failed today.

**Path A — the label event — structurally cannot fire for scheduled work.**

`create-work-item.mjs:107` passes the status label *in the POST body*:

```js
labels: [blocked ? BLOCKED : READY, ...(opts.urgent ? [URGENT] : [])],
```

An issue created *with* a label emits `issues: opened`. The executor subscribes to `issues: [labeled]` only. So a freshly-created standing item never raises the event that would dispatch an executor for it. The workflow's own comment calls this path "latency sugar" on top of the drain — but for the main case it isn't sugar, it's absent. That's why there were **zero** executor runs today despite nine `task:ready` labels at 04:56:57–04:57:00. (The historical `issues`-triggered runs you can see in the log all fired on labels *added* later — mostly `needs-human` — which is why they show `skipped`.)

**Path B — the drain gate — failed its read, silently, and fails closed.**

From today's scheduler-run log ([run 32691808307](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/actions/runs/32691808307)):

```
04:56:57.9  - created #241 basics/task-janitor [task:ready]
     …             nine items, all ready …
04:57:00.4  - schedule board #127 updated (18 row(s))
04:57:00.8  - nothing pickable — no executor is dispatched this run
```

0.4 seconds after creating nine ready items it concluded nothing was pickable, so the `drain` job was skipped on `pickable != 'true'`. That verdict was wrong: `basics/task-janitor` is `frequency: 'daily'` with **no `schedule_after`**, so it passes every `pickOrder` filter — and when I forced an executor six hours later it picked up and completed the entire batch.

The mechanism is `listOpenWorkItems` ([read.mjs:33](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/blob/main/.claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/queue/read.mjs#L33)):

```js
const { status, json } = await gh(`/repos/${repo}/issues?state=open&…`);
if (status !== 200 || !Array.isArray(json) || json.length === 0) break;
```

A non-200 and an empty queue are the same outcome — an empty array, no log, no error. So the gate cannot distinguish *"there is no work"* from *"I could not read the work"*, and it treats both as "don't dispatch". Whether today's read was a swallowed non-200 (nine writes in 25 seconds, then an immediate list) or a stale read-after-write, the shape is the same and the code makes it invisible either way.

**And the blast radius changed last week.** The scheduler used to run hourly — runs 121–144 are ~1h apart through 08-23 04:50. Claudinite #1230 cut it to `11 4,16 * * *`. Under the old cadence a missed drain cost ≤1h and nobody noticed; now it costs ~12h. The bug is probably old; the cadence change is what made it matter.

## Issue 2 — forced it

I dispatched the executor on `main`. [Run 32721708408](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/actions/runs/32721708408) drained the whole backlog in about 55 seconds:

```
#241 task-janitor  → task:done      #245 fleet-usage   → task:done (PR #252 landed)
#243 fleet-pack-seeds → task:done   #247 usage-fold    → task:done
#244 fleet-roster  → task:done      #249 tidy-issues   → obsolete
#248 update        → agent (handed off, PR #253)
```

The janitor's own health line:

```
task-janitor [#241]: health: 12 open work item(s) — 0 blocked, 4 ready, 1 executing,
0 with an agent, 7 needs-human; this run escalated 0 stale, reclaimed 0 dead agent
claim(s), surfaced 0 stuck dependency(ies), repaired 0 stateless item(s)
```

**This does not yet answer your question, and I want to be straight about why.** Shepherd had **zero** agent claims — all 39 blown leashes are in ten *other* repos, and the janitor is scoped to its own repo. It reclaimed nothing because there was nothing here to reclaim. What it does prove is that the janitor is healthy, that it's `code_work` (the run said "no agent was needed" — no model invocation at all), and that it completes in under a second once picked up. Every one of those ten repos has its own `basics/task-janitor` queued and unpicked by the identical gate — e.g. [ClaudiniteWebsite #289](https://github.com/missingbulb/ClaudiniteWebsite/issues/289), ready since 05:07 alongside its 7 blown claims.

One thing I did wrong: I added `task:urgent` to #241 to steer the pick, and that write landed just after the engine closed the item, replacing its terminal `task:done`. I've restored it. The steer was unnecessary anyway — the executor had already reached it.

## Issue 3 — why the janitor is central, and whether the dispatcher should do this

Your instinct is right, and the codebase already agrees with you — it made exactly this move once and stopped.

From [`queue-sweep.mjs`](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/blob/main/.claudinite/shared/packs/basics/tasks/task-janitor/queue-sweep.mjs)'s own header:

> the executing-leash reclaim moved to the SCHEDULER RUN — a deterministic label rule, serialized and hourly, which recovers a dead executor's item in ~2h instead of ~25h.

That's the precedent. The executing-leash reclaim used to live in the janitor, took ~25h, and was moved into the dispatcher where it takes ~2h. **The remaining three rules were left behind, and the reasoning for leaving them no longer holds.**

**The structural problem is circularity.** The janitor's recovery is itself queued work. For a stuck item to be reclaimed, the scheduler must instantiate a janitor item, the gate must ready it, the drain must dispatch an executor, and the executor must pick it. So the mechanism that recovers stuck work *is* stuck work, and it fails in exactly the conditions it exists to handle. Today is the clean demonstration: pickup broke, and the janitor was precisely as stuck as the 39 items it would have reclaimed.

It's worse for the dead-agent rule specifically. **The recovery shares a failure mode with the failure.** Rule B exists because agent sessions die — and the reclaim was, until this design, gated behind the same pickup pipeline those agents depend on.

**"Must we wait for a long delay to get better analysis?" — no, because no analysis is being bought.** The janitor's header claims its rules need "judgment or a longer horizon". That's true of exactly one of them:

| Rule | What it computes | Needs a session? | Eligible for the dispatcher |
|---|---|---|---|
| B — dead agent (3h leash) | `updated_at` vs a clock, on labels | No — pure function, zero I/O | **Yes**, identical in shape to the reclaim already moved |
| A — stale ready (2 periods) | clock + `frequency` from the declarations | No — the run already holds `tasks` | **Yes** |
| D — stateless repair | labels decode to no status, plus one confirm re-read | No | **Yes** |
| C — stuck dependency | must read each `Blocked-by` target's state | Extra API calls; comments only | Leave it — genuinely a longer horizon |

None of A, B or D diagnoses anything. They relabel to `needs-human` and stop. The 12-hour wait buys zero extra insight — it's pure latency in front of a clock comparison.

**And the marginal cost is near zero.** `announcePickable` already fetches the entire open queue on every scheduler run, for the drain gate. Rules A, B and D are pure functions over that same array. The dispatcher would need no extra reads, no executor, no agent, no model call — only the label writes when something is actually stuck. Recovery latency would drop from *"whenever an agent-run task happens to get picked up"* to *"the next cron fire"*, and would stop depending on the very pipeline it repairs.

The counter-argument in the header — "recovery still happens once, in one place per rule, in code, and never as a sweep inside a session that is executing something" — is satisfied by moving them. Each rule still lives in `janitor-rules.mjs` as a pure function with one caller; only the *shell* changes from a queued task to the scheduler run. That's precisely how the executing-leash reclaim was moved.

The one thing I'd fix ahead of all of it, though, is the gate itself. Moving the rules into the scheduler run doesn't help if the run's read of the queue can fail silently and be read as "nothing to do" — that single swallowed non-200 currently disables both the drain *and* would disable any recovery you site there.

To actually answer "is the janitor the solution to those 39", I need to run one in a repo that has blown claims. That reaches the world in repos we haven't touched this session, so:

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files and comment-only changes.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-branch-status: Assess one branch's landed status — merged, already-in-main, superseded, orphaned, or genuine unmerged work — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single branch is safe to delete, judging by content not the ref's name (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-branches task hands you branches to assess).
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
- writing-migration-plans: Where a plan and a design live, and how to order a plan's phases so nothing stalls mid-run — the plan is a tracking issue (never a plan document in the repo), the design doc carries only the end state with rationale and alternatives; front-load the out-of-band setup, write ALL the code including the cleanup and take one approval for the stack, then chain every execution step to the verification of the one before it as a queued continuation, and keep the tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan — including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file — and when working through a plan's tracking issue.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.mjs or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one — Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch
- docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx files) or Word templates (.dotx files). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, performing find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file, use this skill. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or general coding tasks unrelated to document generation.
- import-memory: Import a memory export from another AI assistant into Claude's memory — conversationally, additively, and with the content treated as data.
- morning: Render the user's morning brief as a styled HTML artifact, or set it up as a recurring weekday task. Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead.
- pdf: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill.
- pptx: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email or summary); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user mentions "deck," "slides," "presentation," or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. If a .pptx or .potx file needs to be opened, created, or touched, use this skill.
- skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- xlsx: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved.

teeth') to the compounding loop: it grows from your work, prose is

executable-requirements workflow; the pack anatomy gains its manifest

slots and all four mechanism animations are unchanged; the dark
