content.text:
The ClaudiniteWebsite run is still draining with the janitor as its last item — I'll report that result when it lands. Everything else is settled.

## Issue 1 — why the janitor items aren't picked up

The executor workflow carries **no cron**. It has exactly two delivery paths, and both failed.

**Path (b), the label event, cannot fire for scheduled work at all.** `create-work-item.mjs:107` sets the status label *inline in the create call* — `labels: [blocked ? BLOCKED : READY, …]` — and `createIssue` sends it on `POST /repos/{repo}/issues`. An issue created with labels emits `issues: opened`, never `issues: labeled`, and the executor subscribes only to `labeled`. So a freshly-instantiated standing item never raises the event that would deliver it. The evidence matches: nine `task:ready` labels present at 04:56:57–04:57:00 today, **zero** executor runs today. Every historical `issues`-triggered run was `skipped` — those fired on some *other* label added later — and the two that actually executed were `fleet-baseline` items created by hand from a checkout. The workflow's own header calls this path "latency sugar" over the drain, i.e. redundancy. **The redundancy is structurally absent for exactly the items the scheduler makes each period**, which leaves the drain gate as the sole delivery.

**Path (a), the drain gate, then failed.** From today's scheduler log ([run 32691808307](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/actions/runs/32691808307)):

```
04:56:57  - created #241 basics/task-janitor [task:ready]
          … nine items …
04:57:00  - schedule board #127 updated (18 row(s))
04:57:00  - nothing pickable — no executor is dispatched this run
```

`announcePickable` re-reads the queue 0.4s after those nine creates and finds nothing ready; the drain job's `if: needs.scheduler-run.outputs.pickable == 'true'` skips. Those items were genuinely pickable — my forced executor picked and completed every one of them, and `basics/task-janitor` is `frequency: 'daily'` with no `schedule_after`, so it passes every `pickOrder` filter. **The gate's read was wrong, not the queue empty.**

Why the read was wrong I can narrow to two candidates but not separate them, **because the code cannot separate them either**: `listOpenWorkItems` ([read.mjs:30–43](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/blob/main/.claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/queue/read.mjs#L30)) breaks its page loop on `status !== 200` and returns whatever it accumulated — so an API refusal or throttle is indistinguishable from an empty queue, silently, with no log line. The other candidate is read-after-write staleness on the issues list. The file's header explains it uses the list API *because* search is eventually consistent, but never claims the list is read-your-writes.

**What made a latent bug bite today:** the cadence change. Runs 121–144 were hourly through 08-23 04:50; the cron is now `11 4,16 * * *` — Claudinite #1230, in your own 08-22 digest as "cut fleet-wide cron scheduling from hourly to twice a day". At hourly, a missed dispatch cost ≤1h and was invisible. At twice a day it costs ≤12h, and today it cost the whole day.

Unrelated but standing in every run: `could not read CLAUDINITE_TASKS_SUSPEND_ALL live (403)` — the Actions token lacks variables-read, so a suspend hold only reaches a running drain at its next start.

## Issue 2 — forced it

Shepherd's queue drained completely. The janitor ran as **`code_work` — "no agent was needed"** — and reported ([#241](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/issues/241)):

```
health: 12 open work item(s) — 0 blocked, 4 ready, 1 executing, 0 with an agent, 7 needs-human;
this run escalated 0 stale, reclaimed 0 dead agent claim(s), surfaced 0 stuck dependency(ies),
repaired 0 stateless item(s)
```

Shepherd had zero agent claims, so nothing to reclaim — **that proves the janitor runs, not that it clears the 39.** And the janitor is repo-scoped: Shepherd's can never touch another repo's items. Hence the ClaudiniteWebsite run, still in flight.

The rest of the batch landed too: fleet-usage merged [PR #252](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/pull/252), update opened [PR #253](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/pull/253) and handed off to an agent, tidy-issues went obsolete.

One error of mine to flag: I added `task:urgent` to #241 to jump the queue, and the write landed ~30s *after* the engine had already closed it, replacing its terminal `task:done` with `task:ready, task:urgent`. I restored `task:done`. No functional impact — closed items aren't read by the queue — but it was mine, not the engine's.

## Issue 3 — why the janitor is so central, and whether the dispatcher should do this

**The design already agrees with you, and already did it once.** From `queue-sweep.mjs`'s own header:

> the executing-leash reclaim moved to the SCHEDULER RUN — a deterministic label rule, serialized and hourly, which recovers a dead executor's item in ~2h instead of ~25h

That is precisely the move you're proposing, already made for one rule. Three were left behind on the stated grounds that they need "judgment or a longer horizon". That reasoning doesn't survive contact with the code:

| Rule | Needs | Judgment? |
|---|---|---|
| A — stale ready | clock + task frequency | none; the scheduler already holds `tasks` |
| B — dead agent | clock + labels | none; `deadAgentItems(open, now)` is pure |
| D — stateless repair | labels + one confirm re-read | none |
| C — stuck dependency | states of `Blocked-by` targets | genuinely longer horizon — and it only comments |

A, B and D are pure clock rules over the very array `announcePickable` **already fetches**. They perform no diagnosis — they relabel to `needs-human` so a *person* can diagnose. **So the long delay buys no better analysis. There is no analysis.**

The deeper problem is circularity: **the mechanism that recovers stuck work is itself queued work.** The janitor must be instantiated, readied, dispatched, picked and run before it can rescue anything. Today that chain broke at "dispatched" — so the janitor was exactly as stuck as the 39 items it would have reclaimed. Worse, Rule B recovers *dead agent claims* specifically; if agent invocation is the thing degrading, the janitor is among the least likely things to complete. The recovery shares a failure mode with the failure.

And the janitor gave the game away itself: `Code-work did this run's work; no agent was needed.` It doesn't need to be a task at all.

So: **yes, the dispatcher can and should do short-term recovery.** Move A, B and D into `scheduler-run.mjs` beside the existing executing-leash reclaim, over the array it already reads; leave C in the janitor. Marginal cost is three pure function calls, plus writes only when something is actually stuck.

Two adjacent fixes I'd bundle:

- **`listOpenWorkItems` must not return `[]` for a failed read.** A *delivery* gate should fail open — a spurious executor run costs pennies, a missed one costs 12 hours.
- **Restore real redundancy on delivery** — subscribe the executor to `issues: opened` as well, or apply the status label in a second call after creation so `labeled` actually fires.

> ⚠️ Still open: ClaudiniteWebsite's forced executor ([run 32722656429](https://github.com/missingbulb/ClaudiniteWebsite/actions/runs/32722656429)) is on its last item — the janitor — and its 7 blown claims are untouched so far; I'll report the reclaim result when it lands. Root cause of issue 1 is narrowed to two candidates that the code itself cannot distinguish, because the read fails silently. Nothing filed upstream yet — say the word and I'll open the Claudinite issues for the drain-gate fix, the fail-open read, and moving rules A/B/D into the scheduler run.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files and comment-only changes.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
- git-github-advanced: Git/GitHub procedures beyond the baseline lifecycle. Use for commit layering, recovering a branch after a squash-merge, CI-trigger rules, GitHub Actions gotchas, or merge-relocation traps.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- merge-to-main: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-branch-status: Assess one branch's landed status — merged, already-in-main, superseded, orphaned, or genuine unmerged work — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single branch is safe to delete, judging by content not the ref's name (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-branches task hands you branches to assess).
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
- writing-migration-plans: Where a plan and a design live, and how to order a plan's phases so nothing stalls mid-run — the plan is a tracking issue (never a plan document in the repo), the design doc carries only the end state with rationale and alternatives; front-load the out-of-band setup, write ALL the code including the cleanup and take one approval for the stack, then chain every execution step to the verification of the one before it as a queued continuation, and keep the tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan — including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file — and when working through a plan's tracking issue.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.mjs or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.

Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. - simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.

## Where the stuck tasks stand

**Net reclaimed: 0 of the 39.** The janitor still hasn't been observed reclaiming a single blown agent claim.

**Shepherd** — healthy. Queue fully drained, janitor ran clean, but it had zero agent claims so it had nothing to reclaim. Still an unanswered question, not a passing test.

**ClaudiniteWebsite** — the janitor crashed, and your note explains why. The blob at the failing commit is byte-identical to `main` (`8bf301ec`) and contains no `claudinite-tasks` import, so the missing module was never in the commit — it came from the **working tree**. In the same executor process, `claudinite-lifecycle/update` ran *first*:

```
11:37:19  update: engine — needs-human: the converged tree FAILED its self-test
11:37:25  update: opened PR #294 … left open and labelled needs-human
11:37:33  code_work basics/task-janitor [#289] → ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND
```

Update converged the in-flight canon into the checkout, its self-test correctly caught that the tree wasn't intact, and it correctly refused to land it. But **the same job kept running later tasks against that converged tree**, and the janitor was next in line. Its 7 blown claims are untouched.

The ordering was pure luck — `pickOrder` sorts by urgent, then a random draw. Shepherd happened to draw the janitor *before* update (11:26:27 vs 11:27:11) and its converge passed self-test anyway. ClaudiniteWebsite drew update first and got the poisoned tree.

**The other 9 repos** carrying the remaining 32 claims are untouched — still queued and unpicked behind the drain-gate bug from the last turn.

## What my forced runs left behind

I made ClaudiniteWebsite marginally worse, and you should know it:

- [#289](https://github.com/missingbulb/ClaudiniteWebsite/issues/289) is now `task:needs-human-failure` — a **blocking** park, so that repo's janitor lane is held and won't re-file even once the migration lands. It'll need the label cleared by hand.
- [#292](https://github.com/missingbulb/ClaudiniteWebsite/issues/292) / [PR #294](https://github.com/missingbulb/ClaudiniteWebsite/pull/294) parked `needs-human` — that one is the update task working correctly.

Both would likely have happened at the 16:11 cron anyway; I just brought them forward.

Nothing filed upstream, no code changed, no other repo touched.

> ⚠️ Still open, parked until the migration lands: 39 blown agent claims, 0 reclaimed — the janitor has still never been seen doing the thing we're counting on it for. Two follow-ups queued behind the migration: clear the false blocking park on ClaudiniteWebsite [#289](https://github.com/missingbulb/ClaudiniteWebsite/issues/289), and the finding that a failed converge leaves the working tree broken for every task later in the same executor run — which is a real bug independent of this migration, and worth filing once things are quiet.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. ## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.

- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files and comment-only changes.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files and comment-only changes.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

attachment.content:
- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
- git-github-advanced: Git/GitHub procedures beyond the baseline lifecycle. Use for commit layering, recovering a branch after a squash-merge, CI-trigger rules, GitHub Actions gotchas, or merge-relocation traps.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- merge-to-main: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-branch-status: Assess one branch's landed status — merged, already-in-main, superseded, orphaned, or genuine unmerged work — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single branch is safe to delete, judging by content not the ref's name (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-branches task hands you branches to assess).
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
- writing-migration-plans: Where a plan and a design live, and how to order a plan's phases so nothing stalls mid-run — the plan is a tracking issue (never a plan document in the repo), the design doc carries only the end state with rationale and alternatives; front-load the out-of-band setup, write ALL the code including the cleanup and take one approval for the stack, then chain every execution step to the verification of the one before it as a queued continuation, and keep the tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan — including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file — and when working through a plan's tracking issue.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.mjs or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one — Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch
- docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx files) or Word templates (.dotx files). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, performing find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file, use this skill. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or general coding tasks unrelated to document generation.
- import-memory: Import a memory export from another AI assistant into Claude's memory — conversationally, additively, and with the content treated as data.
- morning: Render the user's morning brief as a styled HTML artifact, or set it up as a recurring weekday task. Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead.
- pdf: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill.
- pptx: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email or summary); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user mentions "deck," "slides," "presentation," or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. If a .pptx or .potx file needs to be opened, created, or touched, use this skill.
- skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- xlsx: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved.

* Declare create-extractor daily, which is what it already runs at

`hourly` is a retired frequency token. It has resolved to `daily` since the
retirement: the canon normalizes a retired token at the declaration door, so
the anchor, the janitor's stale-ready bound and the precondition's signal
window have all read daily regardless of what the line said. The comment
beside it promised "minutes, not overnight", which stopped being true then.

Polling is the wrong shape for this task at all — a request arriving is an
event, and the right trigger is the issue itself. Until that flow exists a
slow implementation cycle is the accepted trade, so the declaration now says
daily plainly rather than asking for a cadence it does not get.

This also unblocks missingbulb/Claudinite#1234, which empties the legacy
frequency map; this was the last declaration in the fleet naming a retired
token, and would have failed contract validation once that lands.

Refs #1060

* Move the declaration's own test to daily with it

The contract test pinned `frequency: 'hourly'`, so it failed the moment the
declaration told the truth. The pin is right to exist — it stops the cadence
drifting back to a token the queue will not honour — so it moves with the
decision rather than being loosened.

The task surface moved out of the vendored engine into its own pack (#1317).

The declaration was never written for this repo. The vendor set ships the pack's
files whether or not they are declared, so the live workflows keep resolving —
but `isActive` reads the literal list, so undeclared the pack is mounted and
inert: its tasks stop being discovered and the queue goes quiet with nothing red

* Declare create-extractor daily, which is what it already runs at

`hourly` is a retired frequency token. It has resolved to `daily` since the
retirement: the canon normalizes a retired token at the declaration door, so
the anchor, the janitor's stale-ready bound and the precondition's signal
window have all read daily regardless of what the line said. The comment
beside it promised "minutes, not overnight", which stopped being true then.

Polling is the wrong shape for this task at all — a request arriving is an
event, and the right trigger is the issue itself. Until that flow exists a
slow implementation cycle is the accepted trade, so the declaration now says
daily plainly rather than asking for a cadence it does not get.

This also unblocks missingbulb/Claudinite#1234, which empties the legacy
frequency map; this was the last declaration in the fleet naming a retired
token, and would have failed contract validation once that lands.

Refs #1060

* Move the declaration's own test to daily with it

The contract test pinned `frequency: 'hourly'`, so it failed the moment the
declaration told the truth. The pin is right to exist — it stops the cadence
drifting back to a token the queue will not honour — so it moves with the
decision rather than being loosened.

* Repoint the queue workflows at the claudinite-tasks mount

The task surface moved out of the vendored engine into a pack, so every `run:`
line moves from `.claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/…` to
`.claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-tasks/…`. This repo's mount already carries
the pack, and the canon keeps shims at the old paths until it retires them, so
both paths are live right now and this lands on its own.

Regenerated from the canon's stubs by the tasks pack's own
`converge-workflows.mjs` — the same code that scaffolds these files — rather
than hand-edited, so this is exactly what the pack says this repo should carry.
The cron is unchanged: it is hashed from the repo's full name and its own
`taskScheduler.dailyHour`, so regenerating reproduces it. The executor's secret
names are unchanged too, regenerated from this repo's own declarations.

`.github/workflows/` is the one directory a converge cannot write, which is why
this arrives as a pull request.

Refs missingbulb/Claudinite#1331

* Drop the executor's comment about what not to put in it

Regenerated from the canon's stub after it lost the paragraph explaining why the
workflow does not serialise the whole secrets context. That is a note about an
edit rather than about the file in front of the reader, and it is pure freight
here: this file is vendored verbatim and nothing reads its comments. The reason
lives beside the code that stamps the secret list, in the pack's
converge-workflows.mjs.

* Claudinite update: engine v60820.1 → v60823.1 and 12 packs upgraded

* Deliver withheld workflow files and fix stale .claudinite-checks.json refs

The update flow could not write .github/workflows/ with its GITHUB_TOKEN, so
it staged claudinite-executor.yml and claudinite-scheduler.yml under
.claudinite/pending-workflows/ for this apply-stage run to move into place
byte-for-byte.

The same run renamed .claudinite-checks.json to .claudinite-settings.json;
this repo's own docs (CLAUDE.md, the gcec local pack, product-wiki READMEs)
still pointed at the old name and are updated to match.

Refs #1029

* Accept the adoption-answers-pending false positive from this rename

The adopt-pack check's base/head pairing (checks.mjs -> work.mjs jsonPair /
readBase) reads both sides of the settings file at the same literal filename,
with no rename-awareness. On this exact branch -- the one that renames
.claudinite-checks.json to .claudinite-settings.json -- that makes every
already-declared pack look newly added, so every pre-existing pending
adoption question (product-wiki, executable-requirements,
claude-code-web-users-support -- none of it caused by this update) trips as
a blocking new-pack omission.

Waived with a dated, cited reason rather than fabricating answers to
adoption questions I have no authority to answer on the owner's behalf.

Regenerated from the canon's stubs by the tasks pack's own
`converge-workflows.mjs`, so this is exactly what the pack says this repo should
be carrying — not a hand-edit of five lines.

Two changes arrive together because they live in the same two files, and
`.github/workflows/` moves only through a human-merged PR:

- Every `run:` line moves from `.claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/…` to
  `.claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-tasks/…`. This repo's mount already
  carries the pack, and the legacy shims stay until the canon's L4, so the two
  paths are live at once and this can land on its own.
- The executor's `CLAUDINITE_SECRETS: ${{ toJSON(secrets) }}` becomes the two
  secrets this repo's tasks actually declare. Serialising the whole secrets
  context is the shape GitHub's malicious-workflow detection flags: this repo's
  executor runs have been parking with zero jobs, waiting on a human click that
  an unattended queue can neither absorb nor notice.

The cron is unchanged — it is hashed from the repo's full name and its own
`taskScheduler.dailyHour`, so regenerating reproduces it.

Regenerated from the canon's stubs by the tasks pack's own
`converge-workflows.mjs`, so this is exactly what the pack says this repo should
be carrying — not a hand-edit of five lines.

Two changes arrive together because they live in the same two files, and
`.github/workflows/` moves only through a human-merged PR:

- Every `run:` line moves from `.claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/…` to
  `.claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-tasks/…`. This repo's mount already
  carries the pack, and the legacy shims stay until the canon's L4, so the two
  paths are live at once and this can land on its own.
- The executor's `CLAUDINITE_SECRETS: ${{ toJSON(secrets) }}` becomes the two
  secrets this repo's tasks actually declare. Serialising the whole secrets
  context is the shape GitHub's malicious-workflow detection flags: this repo's
  executor runs have been parking with zero jobs, waiting on a human click that
  an unattended queue can neither absorb nor notice.

The cron is unchanged — it is hashed from the repo's full name and its own
`taskScheduler.dailyHour`, so regenerating reproduces it.

**Totals: 30 blown claims · 9 blocking failures · ~48 R1 decision parks · 3 dead janitors · 2 torn · ~124 parked items open.**

## What the scan actually proves

**The janitor works.** [CrosswordChat #257](https://github.com/missingbulb/CrosswordChat/issues/257) carries the Rule B comment at 11:57:20 — *"has carried `task:agent` for over 3h… Labeling `needs-human`"* — and the same batch landed across 9 repos within 30 seconds. The prior session's "0 of 39 reclaimed" is superseded; that sweep cleared most of them. Rule B escalates to `needs-human-**decision**`, which is *non-blocking*, so the lane frees and the task re-files. Reclaim, not deadlock.

**Three repos missed the sweep because their janitor died in the migration window.** That's the whole explanation for the two oldest backlogs — ClaudiniteWebsite's 7 claims (~33h) and GCEC's 4 (~41h) sat through the 11:57 sweep because the janitor that would have swept them was itself parked `failure` at 11:37–12:00. Two distinct crashes:
- `spawn /bin/sh ENOENT` — GCEC, hitbut. Node throws this when the **`cwd` doesn't exist**, which is exactly what a task-path move produces.
- `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND … packs/claudinite-tasks/dispatch.mjs` — ClaudiniteWebsite.

Both are migration collateral, and the migration has since landed cleanly (`claudinite-tasks/` is present and complete on Shepherd `main`; executor runs at 19:14 and 20:09 are green). **The code is fixed; the parks it left are not** — a `failure` park is the one kind that holds a lane, so those three janitors stay dead until a label is cleared by hand.

**The real generator is R1, and it's a loop.** Nearly every `needs-human-decision` park traces to one defect you already have filed four times over ([Shepherd #179](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/issues/179), [ClaudiniteWebsite #274](https://github.com/missingbulb/ClaudiniteWebsite/issues/274)/[#277](https://github.com/missingbulb/ClaudiniteWebsite/issues/277), [ClaudiniteCanary #239](https://github.com/missingbulb/ClaudiniteCanary/issues/239)): the agent lane cannot converge its own item. Every daily cycle, each agentic task claims, works, abandons, blows the leash, and gets escalated. The janitor is doing its job perfectly — it's just bailing out a lane with a hole in it. Fixing R1 would drain most of that ~48 and stop the rest accruing.

**One genuine unrelated bug:** Shepherd #205 — `fleet-add-missing-packs failed: missingbulb/Shepherd has no readable .claudinite-settings.json (status 404)`. The fleet sweep can't read its *own* repo's settings file.

**Two repos are dark:** HelloWorldFlutterApp and gRatio have no work-item queue at all — not stuck, just never adopted or long dormant.

## Fleet-wide cost measurement, 2026-08-24

A full sweep of all 16 member repos today measured what this defect actually costs. The diagnosis above needs no correction — it predicted the observed behaviour exactly ("sits stuck wearing `task:agent` until the janitor's 3h agent-leash reclaims it"). What follows is the scale.

**This is the single largest generator of stuck work in the fleet.**

| Measure | Count |
|---|---|
| Open `needs-human` parks across the fleet | ~124 |
| …of those, `task:needs-human-decision` traceable to this defect | **~48** |
| Dead `task:agent` claims awaiting the next janitor pass | **30**, across 12 repos |

The loop is self-sustaining and runs once per task per day: the agent claims the item → does the work correctly → cannot converge → abandons → 3h leash expires → janitor Rule B escalates to `needs-human-decision` → the lane frees → the task re-files tomorrow → repeat. Every cycle mints a fresh park that a person must read and clear by hand.

Two things worth noting for whoever fixes this:

**The work is not lost — only the convergence is.** [CrosswordChat #257](https://github.com/missingbulb/CrosswordChat/issues/257) is a clean specimen: the agent enumerated seven claims, probed them, correctly identified a proxy-level `EGRESS_BLOCKED` as a policy denial rather than retrying it, wrote up a complete verdict — and then could not close its own item. The escalation comment landed 7h later. That is a fully successful task execution parked as if it failed.

**The janitor is working correctly and is not the problem.** Rule B fired fleet-wide at 11:57:20Z today and reclaimed the backlog across nine repos within 30 seconds. It escalates to `needs-human-decision`, which is non-blocking, so lanes free and tasks re-file as designed. It is bailing out a lane with a hole in it, at one bail per task per day.

### Consolidating the duplicate filings

Four member repos each independently filed this same defect, which is itself a signal of how often sessions hit it:

- [Shepherd #179](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/issues/179) — "converge-item.mjs needs GITHUB_TOKEN, which MCP-only agent sessions don't have"
- [ClaudiniteWebsite #274](https://github.com/missingbulb/ClaudiniteWebsite/issues/274) — "Canon defect: converge-item.mjs cannot run session-side"
- [ClaudiniteWebsite #277](https://github.com/missingbulb/ClaudiniteWebsite/issues/277) — "…from a routine-fired Claude Code Web session"
- [ClaudiniteCanary #239](https://github.com/missingbulb/ClaudiniteCanary/issues/239) — "no MCP-compatible agent-lane path for step 6"

Plus #1133 in this repo, which is the same break in the same script from the token angle.

This issue (#1149) has the fullest diagnosis and the right proposed shape — the `deliver-pr.md` / `land-pr.mjs` split mirrored for convergence — so it should be the one that owns the fix; the rest are evidence that it is worth doing.

* Repoint the queue workflows at the claudinite-tasks mount

The task surface moved out of the vendored engine into a pack, so every `run:`
line moves from `.claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/…` to
`.claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-tasks/…`. This repo's mount already carries
the pack, and the canon keeps shims at the old paths until it retires them, so
both paths are live right now and this lands on its own.

Regenerated from the canon's stubs by the tasks pack's own
`converge-workflows.mjs` — the same code that scaffolds these files — rather
than hand-edited, so this is exactly what the pack says this repo should carry.
The cron is unchanged: it is hashed from the repo's full name and its own
`taskScheduler.dailyHour`, so regenerating reproduces it. The executor's secret
names are unchanged too, regenerated from this repo's own declarations.

`.github/workflows/` is the one directory a converge cannot write, which is why
this arrives as a pull request.

Refs missingbulb/Claudinite#1331

* Drop the executor's comment about what not to put in it

Regenerated from the canon's stub after it lost the paragraph explaining why the
workflow does not serialise the whole secrets context. That is a note about an
edit rather than about the file in front of the reader, and it is pure freight
here: this file is vendored verbatim and nothing reads its comments. The reason
lives beside the code that stamps the secret list, in the pack's
converge-workflows.mjs.

Refs missingbulb/Claudinite#1331

The deploy reached production, applied the migrations, and then failed: the
account had never registered a workers.dev subdomain, so `wrangler deploy` had
nowhere to publish to. It asks for one interactively, and on a runner that is a
failed deploy — after the schema has already moved.

The preflight said production was ready, because it only ever asked wrangler,
and wrangler has no command for this. It now reads the account directly for the
subdomain — a GET, the only one here, and the whole reason the wrangler runner
stays closed to everything else.

The failure that led here also arrived with its actionable half missing: the
URL wrangler sends you to sits after a blank line, and the reason stopped at the
first one. It now crosses a single blank and stops at two.

The `CCR_ROUTINE_TOKEN` secret is set in this repo, but
.github/workflows/claudinite-executor.yml never passed it: the
`# claudinite:secrets` marker had nothing stamped under it, so the
executor job's env carried no token and every agentic task parked with
"the Actions secret CCR_ROUTINE_TOKEN ... is not set in this repo".

The correct workflow already existed, staged and undelivered at
.claudinite/pending-workflows/claudinite-executor.yml. A converge cannot
write .github/workflows/ (the Actions token is refused there), so it
withholds the file; the only thing that delivers a staged workflow is the
agentic apply stage — which cannot start without the token the staged file
carries. The fix for the missing token was gated behind the one stage that
needed it, so this repo could not escape on its own.

Moved byte for byte: the delivered file differs from the previous one by
exactly the token line. Every agentic task has been parked since
2026-08-21 and the mount is stuck at engine v60820.1 against canon's
v60823.1; once this lands the agent stage runs and the repo self-heals.

Closes #102

* Spec: the wordmark's two halves are two eras

Refs #98

* Screen lane: a case can capture one element's box

A leaf about one piece of a page — the masthead lockup, say — is proven by a picture of
that piece, not by the whole page around it at 30px. The clip is taken off the full-page
shot in document coordinates, so nothing scrolls and no state is dismissed.

Refs #98

* Wordmark: התבט worn, אויות lacquered

The lockup's carve now carries the product's subject. התבט is set in Frank Ruhl Libre,
letter by letter so each sits a shade off the line, with a fixed-seed noise mask pitting
the ink from the baseline up; אויות is Heebo, tight, filled with a lacquered gradient.
Every screen golden carries the masthead, so all of them are re-rendered.

Closes #98

The first real provision run created three of four resources and reported
success. Two things were wrong with that.

The R2 listing failed with "A request to the Cloudflare API (/accounts/…/
r2/buckets) failed." and nothing else — wrangler puts the code that separates
a missing token scope from a product never enabled on the account on the line
under the marked one, and only the marked one was being read. The reason now
carries its continuation.

And the run went green while production was not ready: the provisioner exits
clean when it declines, which is right, but the preflight after it ran under
`|| true`. The preflight is the honest answer to "did it work"; it now decides
the run.

A concurrency group also queues a second press behind the first, so two runs
cannot both try to create the same resource.

The `CCR_ROUTINE_TOKEN` secret is set in this repo, but
.github/workflows/claudinite-executor.yml never passed it: the
`# claudinite:secrets` marker had nothing stamped under it, so the
executor job's env carried no token and every agentic task parked with
"the Actions secret CCR_ROUTINE_TOKEN ... is not set in this repo".

The correct workflow already existed, staged and undelivered at
.claudinite/pending-workflows/claudinite-executor.yml. A converge cannot
write .github/workflows/ (the Actions token is refused there), so it
withholds the file; the only thing that delivers a staged workflow is the
agentic apply stage — which cannot start without the token the staged file
carries. The fix for the missing token was gated behind the one stage that
needed it, so this repo could not escape on its own.

Moved byte for byte: the delivered file differs from the previous one by
exactly the token line. Every agentic task has been parked since
2026-08-21 and the mount is stuck at engine v60820.1 against canon's
v60823.1; once this lands the agent stage runs and the repo self-heals.

Closes #102

The task surface moved out of the vendored engine into its own pack (#1317).

The declaration was never written for this repo. The vendor set ships the pack's
files whether or not they are declared, so the live workflows keep resolving —
but `isActive` reads the literal list, so undeclared the pack is mounted and
inert: its tasks stop being discovered and the queue goes quiet with nothing red

The first real provision run created three of four resources and reported
success. Two things were wrong with that.

The R2 listing failed with "A request to the Cloudflare API (/accounts/…/
r2/buckets) failed." and nothing else — wrangler puts the code that separates
a missing token scope from a product never enabled on the account on the line
under the marked one, and only the marked one was being read. The reason now
carries its continuation.

And the run went green while production was not ready: the provisioner exits
clean when it declines, which is right, but the preflight after it ran under
`|| true`. The preflight is the honest answer to "did it work"; it now decides
the run.

A concurrency group also queues a second press behind the first, so two runs
cannot both try to create the same resource.

and both deploy origins are readable off the deploys themselves — so neither

both paths are live right now and this lands on its own.

names are unchanged too, regenerated from this repo's own declarations.

this arrives as a pull request.

edit rather than about the file in front of the reader, and it is pure freight
here: this file is vendored verbatim and nothing reads its comments. The reason
lives beside the code that stamps the secret list, in the pack's
converge-workflows.mjs.

The deploy reached production, applied the migrations, and then failed: the
account had never registered a workers.dev subdomain, so `wrangler deploy` had
nowhere to publish to. It asks for one interactively, and on a runner that is a
failed deploy — after the schema has already moved.

and wrangler has no command for this. It now reads the account directly for the
subdomain — a GET, the only one here, and the whole reason the wrangler runner

The first real provision run created three of four resources and reported
success. Two things were wrong with that.

The R2 listing failed with "A request to the Cloudflare API (/accounts/…/
r2/buckets) failed." and nothing else — wrangler puts the code that separates
a missing token scope from a product never enabled on the account on the line
under the marked one, and only the marked one was being read. The reason now
carries its continuation.

And the run went green while production was not ready: the provisioner exits
clean when it declines, which is right, but the preflight after it ran under
`|| true`. The preflight is the honest answer to "did it work"; it now decides
the run.

A concurrency group also queues a second press behind the first, so two runs
cannot both try to create the same resource.

Every resource the account needs is one non-interactive `wrangler … create`,
and both deploy origins are readable off the deploys themselves — so neither
the per-resource dashboard clicking nor the two-pass first deploy was ever
necessary. A `provision` workflow now creates whatever the preflight reports
missing, reads the D1 id back and commits it; the deploy reads each origin
back and hands it to the next step.

The runner is closed by default — it lists, it creates, it deploys — so no
command that removes a database, a bucket, an index or their contents can run,
and only the all-zeros placeholder database id is ever replaced.

# A thin wrapper: every decision lives in the engine modules named in the `run:`
# lines below, which converge nightly — this file does not, so it must not grow
# logic. The cron is a placeholder; bootstrap and the wiring converge rewrite it
# to this repo's hashed minute and its own two anchor hours.
name: Claudinite scheduler

on:
  schedule:
    - cron: '11 4,16 * * *'
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      wake:
        description: 'Task ids to run now (`pack/task` or a bare task name, space-separated) — wakes each one’s standing item regardless of its anchor'
        required: false
        type: string

concurrency:
  group: claudinite-scheduler-run
  cancel-in-progress: false

permissions:
  contents: write
  issues: write
  pull-requests: write
  actions: write

jobs:
  scheduler-run:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      pickable: ${{ steps.run.outputs.pickable }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 24
      - name: Instantiate, ready and reclaim work items
        id: run
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          CLAUDINITE_WAKE: ${{ inputs.wake }}
          CLAUDINITE_TASKS_SUSPEND_ALL: ${{ vars.CLAUDINITE_TASKS_SUSPEND_ALL }}
        run: node .claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/queue/scheduler-run.mjs

  drain:
    needs: scheduler-run
    # An older member workflow maps no such output, and an empty string is not
    # 'true' — so a stale copy keeps dispatching, the previous behavior and safe.
    if: needs.scheduler-run.outputs.pickable == 'true'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      actions: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 24
      - name: Start an executor for what this run readied
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}

## What's in them

**176 open work items** across the 14 active repos (HelloWorldFlutterApp and gRatio have no queue). Every row carries a reason code, whether it holds a task lane, and its age.

| Code | Reason | N | What it means for you |

| R1 | Agent lane couldn't converge its own item | **53** | Canon [#1149](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1149). Non-blocking, but mints a new park every cycle |

Of 176 items, **14 actually hold a lane**. The other 162 are either self-healing, dead pointers, or a genuine queue for your judgement.

## What changed while I built it

The three dead janitors are fixed and **all 12 stale claims behind them are swept**:

- **hitbut** [#108](https://github.com/missingbulb/hitbut/issues/108) → reclaimed 22:07:35
- **ClaudiniteWebsite** [#239](https://github.com/missingbulb/ClaudiniteWebsite/issues/239)–[#262](https://github.com/missingbulb/ClaudiniteWebsite/issues/262), 7 items → 22:08:58–22:09:11 (some ~34h old)
- **GoogleCalendarEventCreator** [#979](https://github.com/missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator/issues/979), [#980](https://github.com/missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator/issues/980), [#1036](https://github.com/missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator/issues/1036), [#1038](https://github.com/missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator/issues/1038) → 22:09:15–22:09:22 (~41h old)

Zero `task:agent` left in any of the three. **Rule B is now confirmed working end-to-end**, watched live rather than inferred.

## Two corrections worth your attention

**My first fix was wrong, and the engine caught it.** I re-labelled the three parked janitor items `task:ready`; all three closed `task:obsolete` instead of running. Their bodies point at `packs/basics/tasks/task-janitor/` — the **pre-migration path** — so the executor correctly retired them as stale pointers. The engine also refuses a hand-made item for a scheduled task outright. The sanctioned lever turned out to be the scheduler's **`wake` input**, which mints a fresh standing item; that's what actually worked.

**The migration left a fleet-wide trap.** Every work item filed before the move still names `basics/task-janitor`. They don't fail loudly — they retire as `obsolete`, which reads like "nothing to do". [MissingBulbWebsite #219](https://github.com/missingbulb/MissingBulbWebsite/issues/219) did exactly this at 14:00 today and I initially misread it as a clean no-op. Any repo whose janitor item predates the migration will silently skip its sweep until the next daily cycle files a fresh one.

I did **not** file the consolidated canon issue you approved — canon already had it twice ([#1149](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1149), [#1133](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1133)). A third would have been noise, so I added the fleet-wide cost measurement to #1149 instead and cross-linked the four member-repo duplicates.

> ⚠️ Still open: **14 lane-blockers** need you — 6 blocking failure parks ([Shepherd #205](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/issues/205) is a real bug: the fleet sweep can't read its own repo's `.claudinite-settings.json`, 404), 2 torn items no janitor rule can see ([Claudinite #1086](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1086), [ClaudiniteCanary #133](https://github.com/missingbulb/ClaudiniteCanary/issues/133)), and 6 bare `needs-human` that decode to failure. **31 retired-id items** are safe to bulk-close whenever you want. The **R1 loop keeps minting ~53 parks** until #1149 is fixed. **11 repos still carry pre-migration janitor pointers** that will skip one sweep each — say the word and I'll fire the `wake` lever across all of them tonight rather than letting them drift a day.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. - **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.

- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files and comment-only changes.
